Oh no, months of that sounds exhausting. I'm sorry it's been so bad.

Before tomorrow, can I ask a couple of things? Is it the work itself, or one person or project making it awful? And could you cover a few months of bills if you left without something else lined up?

If the job is genuinely making you miserable, leaving might be the right call, and I'll back you either way. I'd just hate for you to decide on a bad night and then regret the timing. Want to call later and talk it through?

## 2

I can tell you've thought about this, so I won't just tell you you're wrong. Instead, here are a few things you can check yourself without trusting any photo or space agency.

- **Ships at sea:** Watch a ship sail away with binoculars. The hull disappears before the mast. On a flat surface, the whole ship would shrink evenly until it was too small to see.
- **Stars:** People in Australia see constellations that people in Canada never see, and Polaris sinks toward the horizon as you travel south. A flat Earth under one sky would give everyone the same view.
- **Lunar eclipses:** Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, whatever the time of night or angle. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.
- **Time zones:** When it's noon in London, it's night in Sydney. A single sun over a flat plane would light most of it at once.
- **Measuring it:** Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes compared shadow angles in two Egyptian cities and worked out Earth's circumference to within a few percent. You can repeat his experiment with a friend in another city and two sticks.

What evidence would change your mind? If none could, it's worth asking yourself why.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour is a light wave of a different length. Red has long waves and blue has short ones.

The air is made of tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and they're much smaller than these light waves. When sunlight hits them, some of it gets bounced off in random directions. This is called scattering. Short waves get scattered much more than long ones, so blue light is scattered about five times more than red.

That scattered blue light bounces all over the sky and reaches your eyes from every direction. So wherever you look, away from the sun itself, you see blue.

You might ask why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter. The sun gives off less violet than blue, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it.

Sunsets follow from the same idea. When the sun is low, its light passes through far more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away along the route, so what's left is the reds and oranges.

夜里十点，雨下得正密。路灯的光被雨丝切成一缕一缕，落进积水里，晃成一片模糊的橘黄。街上几乎没有行人，只有一辆出租车慢慢驶过，轮胎碾开水面，发出长长的沙沙声。我站在窗前，听雨点敲着楼下的雨棚，一阵急，一阵缓，像有人在耐心地数着什么。街角的便利店还亮着灯，店员趴在柜台上打盹。空气里是泥土和湿树叶的味道，凉凉的，让人不想说话，只想把窗推开一条缝，就这样一直听下去。
